paragraphs: This paper investigates where backdoor attacks leave their effects inside CLIP. The authors decompose image representations into contributions from individual image patches, attention heads, and multilayer perceptrons across layers. This lets them examine which components change under an attack instead of treating the resulting image representation as a single, opaque output.

Their empirical findings distinguish two attack patterns. Local patch attacks mainly affect attention heads, whereas attacks using global perturbations mainly affect multilayer perceptrons. Affected heads concentrate in the final layer, while affected perceptrons spread across several later layers. Even within the final layer, some heads retain their original roles, such as representing color or location.

These observations motivate defenses that operate during inference: identifying affected heads, repairing their representations, or filtering samples associated with too many affected heads. Experiments support both the component-level findings and the effectiveness of these defenses. The contribution is an empirical connection between the form of an attack, its internal effects, and targeted ways to intervene.
icml-2025-a-closer-look-at-backdoor-atta.tldr: An empirical analysis locates different CLIP backdoor effects in different components and uses those findings to design inference-time defenses.

paragraphs: Predicting chaotic systems far into the future is difficult because small errors grow over time. For many such systems, ergodicity provides another useful target: preserving long-term statistical behavior. Existing approaches use optimal transport to match these statistics, but comparing distributions becomes difficult as the number of dimensions grows.

The paper develops a transformer framework for generating long, stable trajectories of large chaotic systems while preserving ergodicity. Its design draws on the Von Neumann mean ergodic theorem and formulates preservation of long-term statistics in an L2 function space. Changes to the attention mechanism adapt the architecture to learning these large dynamical systems.

The reported experiments show better performance than operator-based and transformer-based methods across five measures covering short-term accuracy and long-term statistics. The authors also introduce a turbulent channel-flow dataset containing 140,000 snapshots and a processed high-dimensional Kolmogorov Flow dataset. Together, the method and benchmarks address both scalable prediction and evaluation of whether generated trajectories retain the statistical behavior of the underlying system.
icml-2025-chaos-meets-attention-transfor.tldr: A modified transformer generates large-scale chaotic trajectories while targeting preservation of their long-term statistics.

paragraphs: A predictive model can compress data well yet lose its advantage once the storage needed for its parameters is counted. Simply shrinking the model can also weaken its predictions and compression. This paper empirically searches for a useful balance between model size and compression quality using ordinary pretrained transformers.

The authors train on 165GB of raw bytes from text, images, audio, and every combination of these modalities. They then compress 1GB of out-of-distribution data per modality. Models with millions of parameters can outperform general-purpose compressors such as gzip and LZMA2, as well as domain-specific compressors, even after parameter storage is included. One audio result reaches a compression ratio of 0.49, compared with 0.54 for FLAC.

Further experiments vary model size, training-data scale, and modality combinations. Small models can compress several modalities effectively when trained for them, but transfer to unseen modalities is generally weak. The findings identify an empirical regime where learned compression is competitive without requiring the parameter budgets of large foundation models.
icml-2025-compression-via-pre-trained-tr.tldr: Small byte-level transformers can outperform conventional compressors even when their parameter storage is counted, though unseen-modality transfer remains weak.

paragraphs: ConceptAttention examines whether multimodal diffusion transformers contain representations that can locate textual concepts within images. Its output is a saliency map: an indication of where a concept appears in an image. The method uses existing attention-layer parameters and requires no additional training, making interpretation a new use of representations already learned by the model.

The central finding concerns where to read information from an attention layer. ConceptAttention constructs contextual concept embeddings and performs linear projections in the layer's output space. These projections produce substantially sharper saliency maps than commonly used cross-attention maps. The result suggests that the output representations contain useful spatial information beyond what those attention maps expose.

The method achieves state-of-the-art results on zero-shot segmentation benchmarks and outperforms 15 other zero-shot interpretability methods on ImageNet-Segmentation. It also works with popular image models and extends to video generation. These findings support the transfer of multimodal diffusion-transformer features to visual tasks such as segmentation, alongside their usefulness for interpreting generated content.
icml-2025-conceptattention-diffusion-tra.tldr: ConceptAttention uses diffusion-transformer attention outputs to locate image concepts without extra training, producing sharper maps and strong zero-shot segmentation results.

paragraphs: When resources permit intervention at only K locations, a forecast must support a selection decision. This paper studies fraction of best possible reach, or BPR, which compares the impact of the recommended locations with the best selection in hindsight. The authors address both how to rank locations and how to train models for this objective.

For probabilistic models that jointly predict event counts across locations, ranking by each location's mean is suboptimal for BPR. The paper develops a better ranking using decision theory. It also addresses a training obstacle: discrete selection produces zero gradients with respect to model parameters, preventing ordinary gradient-based learning from directly improving the selection.

The proposed solution uses perturbed optimizers to make decision-aware training possible. A further objective combines likelihood with a BPR constraint, seeking useful forecasts across all locations alongside strong top-K choices. Applications concern opioid-related fatal overdose mitigation and endangered-wildlife monitoring. The contribution connects the forecasting objective to the particular resource-allocation measure used to judge decisions.
icml-2025-decision-aware-training-of-spa.tldr: The paper develops ranking and training methods that align probabilistic forecasts with the impact of selecting K intervention sites.

paragraphs: Residual connections carry information between transformer layers, but combining earlier outputs through simple summation can dilute useful signals. DeepCrossAttention changes how the model combines information across depth. Its goal is to let later computation draw selectively on earlier layers instead of relying only on an undifferentiated sum.

The method learns weights that depend on the current input, allowing different earlier layers to contribute differently for different examples. It also introduces cross-attention across depth, enabling richer interactions among layer outputs. These two changes make the route through earlier representations adaptive while adding relatively few parameters.

In language-modeling experiments, DeepCrossAttention improves perplexity for a given training time and reaches the same model quality up to three times faster, with an example parameter increase of 0.2%. A theoretical result also supports a better accuracy–model-size trade-off when the ratio of collective layer ranks to ambient dimension is below a critical threshold. That condition matters: the theoretical advantage is tied to a stated relationship between layer structure and representation size.
icml-2025-deepcrossattention-superchargi.tldr: DeepCrossAttention adaptively combines transformer layers, improving reported language-model training efficiency with little parameter overhead.

paragraphs: Preference alignment methods often assume a particular mathematical model of how people choose between outputs. This paper argues that assumptions such as the Bradley–Terry model can create statistical inconsistency: collecting more preference data need not make the learned result converge to the true preferences. The issue concerns the method's eventual target, not just its performance with limited data.

Direct Density Ratio Optimization, or DDRO, instead estimates the ratio between distributions of preferred and unpreferred outputs. This makes the distinction between those distributions the direct learning target. It avoids specifying an explicit model of the human preference process as an intermediate step.

The authors prove statistical consistency, with convergence to the true preferred distribution as the amount of data grows, regardless of the underlying preference structure. They also report better experimental performance than existing approaches. The theoretical result gives an asymptotic justification for the method, while the experiments support its practical promise. Together, these contributions address both the statistical formulation of alignment and its observed effectiveness.
icml-2025-direct-density-ratio-optimizat.tldr: DDRO directly estimates preferred-to-unpreferred output density ratios and is proved statistically consistent without an explicit human preference model.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows describe probability distributions by transforming samples from a simple starting distribution. Standard versions struggle with heavy tails, where unusually extreme values retain substantial probability. This matters for both density estimation and variational inference. A common response is to start with a heavy-tailed distribution, so the model receives those properties at its input.

The authors argue that this remedy can make neural-network optimization difficult and lead to poor performance. Their alternative, tail transform flow, starts from a Gaussian distribution and adds a final transformation capable of producing heavy tails. The design changes where tail behavior enters the model: it is introduced at the output rather than imposed on the input.

Experiments show that this approach outperforms current methods, particularly for targets with many dimensions or greater tail weight. The findings support separating the choice of an input distribution for optimization from the tail behavior needed in the final distribution. The reported advantage is especially relevant to the demanding targets identified in those experiments.
icml-2025-flexible-tails-for-normalizing.tldr: Tail transform flows combine a Gaussian base with a final heavy-tail transformation, improving reported performance especially on high-dimensional or heavier-tailed targets.

paragraphs: UNet-style models use skip connections to bring information into the decoding process for medical image segmentation. This paper identifies two weaknesses in those connections: limited interaction between features at different scales and reliance on simple addition or concatenation. Improving the encoder or decoder alone does not directly address how these features are combined.

FuseUNet reframes decoding as an initial value problem, with skip connections serving as discrete nodes in that process. Drawing on linear multistep methods, the authors develop an adaptive ordinary differential equation approach for combining information across scales. The numerical-method perspective supplies a structured way to integrate features rather than treating each connection as a simple merge.

The fusion method is independent of the particular encoder and decoder, allowing its use in different U-Net-like architectures. Experiments cover cardiac, kidney, brain-tumor, and skin-lesion segmentation datasets. The reported results show better feature utilization and fewer network parameters while maintaining high performance. The contribution is therefore a reusable change to feature integration within this family of segmentation models.
icml-2025-fuseunet-a-multi-scale-feature.tldr: FuseUNet uses an adaptive differential-equation formulation to combine multiscale skip features while reducing parameters and maintaining high segmentation performance.

paragraphs: Contrastive representation learning constructs training tuples from examples, but practical datasets often reuse the same labeled points in many tuples. This reuse makes the tuples dependent. The paper addresses a mismatch with earlier generalization analyses that assume tuples are independently and identically distributed, even though that assumption fails under this common construction.

The authors derive bounds for supervised contrastive learning in a setting that accounts for these dependencies. Their analysis draws on U-statistics, providing a way to reason about combinations built from a shared pool of observations. The resulting bounds relate the required number of examples in each class to the logarithm of a covering number for that class's learnable representations.

A covering number describes the size of a collection needed to approximate a function class, so the result connects sample needs with representation complexity. The authors then derive excess-risk bounds for linear maps and neural networks. The contribution is a theoretical account of generalization that better reflects reuse of labeled data when constructing contrastive training tuples.
icml-2025-generalization-analysis-for-su.tldr: The paper derives contrastive-learning generalization bounds that account for dependent tuples formed by reusing labeled examples.

paragraphs: Federated learning shares training gradients instead of raw examples, but those gradients can still reveal information about the data. Gradient inversion attacks exploit this exposure to reconstruct private content. This paper asks how that risk extends to multimodal models, where earlier work had largely examined simpler, single-modality tasks such as image classification.

The authors focus on document visual question answering, a vision-language task involving document content. They introduce GI-DQA, a method that reconstructs private document information from gradients. By studying this setting, the work moves the privacy investigation beyond reconstructing a single type of input in a relatively simple prediction task.

Extensive evaluations on state-of-the-art document question-answering models reveal substantial privacy vulnerabilities. The findings show that exchanging gradients can expose sensitive document content even in these more complex multimodal systems. The paper's contribution is both an attack method and evidence that privacy assessments of federated learning need to cover vision-language architectures. It motivates stronger defenses for such systems without presenting gradient sharing itself as a sufficient privacy guarantee.
icml-2025-gradient-inversion-of-multimod.tldr: GI-DQA reconstructs private document content from multimodal model gradients, exposing privacy risks in federated document question answering.

paragraphs: This paper develops a sampler for probability densities whose normalization constant is unknown. It combines continuous normalizing flows with rejection and resampling steps based on importance weights. The motivation is that flow-based movement alone can become trapped in local minima or progress slowly when a target distribution has several modes.

The approach alternates local flow updates with nonlocal resampling. The model itself supplies the proposals used in rejection, avoiding common drawbacks of classical rejection schemes. The authors connect iterative training with regularized velocity fields to a JKO scheme and prove convergence of those fields to the velocity field of a Wasserstein gradient flow.

The resulting model can be trained incrementally, with each step reducing the reverse KL objective. It also supports independent, identically distributed samples and evaluation of the density it generates. Numerical examples include high-dimensional multimodal targets and show accurate results, with significant improvements over the state of the art in almost all tested cases. The method joins a flow-based construction with corrective sampling to address difficult target distributions.
icml-2025-importance-corrected-neural-jk.tldr: Combining continuous flows with importance-based rejection and resampling improves sampling from difficult multimodal densities.

paragraphs: This paper studies how multi-head softmax attention learns to perform linear regression from examples supplied in context. It combines empirical experiments with theoretical analysis to connect the training process to the internal structure of the resulting model. The focus is on explaining how useful computation emerges from gradient-based training with random initialization.

The authors identify recurring patterns in the attention weights: diagonal, homogeneous structure in key-query weights, and last-entry-only, zero-sum structure in output-value weights. Their analysis connects these patterns to an approximate implementation of a debiased gradient-descent predictor. In the studied setting, this predictor outperforms single-head attention and approaches Bayesian optimality up to a proportional factor.

The analysis also extends to covariates with direction-dependent variation and to multiple linear-regression tasks. These extensions examine how the mechanism interacts with different data structures. The central finding is that in-context learning arises through the joint influence of the attention architecture and the data distribution. The paper provides a mechanistic explanation of this interaction in linear regression rather than treating the learned behavior as unexplained prediction ability.
icml-2025-in-context-linear-regression-d.tldr: Learned multi-head attention patterns approximately implement a debiased gradient-descent predictor for in-context linear regression.

paragraphs: LlavaGuard is an open framework for assessing visual content against safety policies using vision-language models. The paper treats this as a task that needs both trained models and a clear process for defining what counts as acceptable content. Its framework includes a customizable safety taxonomy, data preparation, augmentation, and a training setup.

The authors create a multimodal dataset with expert human annotations. Each image receives a safety rating, category, and explanation, giving the safeguard information about both the judgment and its rationale. Additional augmentations support assessments that depend on context. The resulting models range from 0.5 billion to 7 billion parameters and can evaluate content under flexible policies.

Experiments report better accuracy and greater policy flexibility than existing safeguards and vision-language models. The paper also demonstrates large-scale dataset annotation and moderation of text-to-image models. These applications connect the assessment framework to both existing visual collections and generated content. Public release of the dataset, model weights, and training code makes the full framework available for reuse.
icml-2025-llavaguard-an-open-vlm-based-f.tldr: LlavaGuard provides openly available vision-language safeguards trained on expert annotations to assess images under customizable safety policies.

paragraphs: Next-token prediction loss does not reliably reveal whether a model is doing substantial computation. Easy sequences can produce low loss without requiring much reasoning, while unpredictable but irrelevant information can produce high loss. This paper instead measures how well a sequence model can predict its own future internal states.

The authors introduce a prediction-of-hidden-states layer, called PHi, that acts as an information bottleneck along the network's main computational pathway. The design is architecture-agnostic and can operate in a transformer's residual stream. A learned predictive prior enables measurement of the new information gained at each computation step, forming the proposed complexity metric.

Empirically, this measure tracks the intuitive complexity of tasks more closely than next-token loss. It predicts the description length of formal languages learned in context, the complexity of mathematical reasoning problems, and the correctness of model-generated reasoning chains. These results support hidden-state predictability as a useful indicator of computation in the examined settings. The evidence is correlational and empirical rather than a universal identification of meaningful reasoning.
icml-2025-measuring-in-context-computati.tldr: Predicting a model's future hidden states yields an empirical measure associated with task complexity and reasoning correctness.

paragraphs: World models help decision-making systems represent how an environment behaves. This paper argues that unstructured representations do not explicitly capture higher-level regions with different dynamics, such as water and land. Structured World Modeling for Policy Optimization, or SWMPO, instead learns a neurosymbolic finite state machine to represent this environmental organization.

Each machine state corresponds to a region with its own dynamics. The synthesis procedure learns this structure without supervision from low-level features in unprocessed, nonvisual data. It extends this style of world modeling beyond the discrete spaces addressed by earlier finite-state-machine approaches, making the representation applicable to continuous-space settings.

The learned machines are expressive enough to support a model-based reinforcement-learning scheme that uses offline data to construct environment-specific world models. Experiments in simulated environments demonstrate advantages in environmental modeling. The contribution is a structured connection between observed low-level behavior and a higher-level model usable for policy optimization. Its reported evidence concerns simulated settings and learning from nonvisual data, which defines the scope of the demonstrated approach.
icml-2025-neurosymbolic-world-models-for.tldr: SWMPO learns finite-state world models from nonvisual offline data to capture regions with distinct dynamics and support policy optimization.

paragraphs: Training neural networks requires memory for accumulated gradients and persistent optimizer state. One way to reduce that cost is to map gradients linearly into a smaller space, perform optimization there, and map the update back using the transpose of the transformation. This paper examines what that procedure means in terms of the model being trained.

The authors show that this transformed-gradient optimization is equivalent to adding a linear adapter to the original parameters and optimizing only the adapter. The two descriptions therefore connect an optimizer-side change with a model-reparameterization change. This equivalence gives a common mathematical interpretation to approaches that can otherwise appear to operate at different parts of training.

For Kronecker-factored transformations, the result establishes an equivalence between GaLore and one-sided LoRA. The qualifier matters because the stated connection concerns that specific transformation structure and adapter form. More broadly, the duality unifies existing memory-efficient training methods and suggests ways to develop new ones. The contribution is an analytical relationship that can guide decisions about training efficiency and memory use.
icml-2025-on-the-duality-between-gradien.tldr: Optimization with linear gradient transformations is equivalent to training additive linear adapters, connecting GaLore and one-sided LoRA under a specific factorization.

paragraphs: Neural algorithmic reasoning trains networks to reproduce the steps of classical algorithms. Much of the earlier work concerns exact algorithms for problems that can be solved in polynomial time. This paper develops a framework for harder problems by drawing on the primal-dual paradigm used to construct efficient approximation algorithms.

The framework represents relationships between primal and dual variables as a bipartite graph. That representation aligns the structure of primal-dual algorithms with graph neural networks, giving the learned system an algorithmic organization to follow. The authors also incorporate optimal solutions from small problem instances to strengthen the model's reasoning beyond learning to imitate approximation procedures alone.

Experiments show that the model can simulate and outperform approximation algorithms across multiple tasks. It also generalizes well in the reported tests to larger graphs and graphs outside the training distribution. Integrations with commercial solvers and applications to real-world datasets demonstrate practical uses. These are empirical results: they support learning useful approximation behavior without asserting that the network becomes an exact solver for all harder problems.
icml-2025-primal-dual-neural-algorithmic.tldr: A primal-dual graph framework helps neural models learn approximation algorithms and empirically improve on them across multiple tasks.

paragraphs: Graph transformers use pairwise computations that can make their computational cost grow quadratically with graph size. This becomes a barrier when learning representations of large graphs. Primphormer addresses that cost by reconsidering the mathematical representation of graph attention rather than only trying to make the existing pairwise computation cheaper.

The authors introduce a primal-dual framework in which conventional graph self-attention is interpreted as a dual representation. They then construct a transformer using the corresponding primal representation, obtaining linear complexity. The change provides an alternative formulation of the attention mechanism with a more favorable scaling pattern.

Theoretical analysis shows that Primphormer is a universal approximator for functions on sequences and graphs, while retaining expressive power for distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs. These results address whether the computational change sacrifices key representation capabilities. Experiments across graph benchmarks report competitive results together with lower memory and computational costs. The paper therefore combines a scaling improvement with theoretical expressiveness results and empirical evidence that the architecture remains useful on graph-learning tasks.
icml-2025-primphormer-efficient-graph-tr.tldr: Primphormer reformulates graph attention through a primal representation to achieve linear complexity while retaining theoretical expressiveness and competitive results.

paragraphs: Shuffling-based gradient methods are widely used because they are simple and work well empirically. Their theoretical guarantees, however, often rely on Lipschitz smoothness, a condition controlling how quickly gradients can change. The authors provide counterexamples showing that this condition need not hold in common machine-learning models, creating a gap between practice and existing analysis.

The paper develops a step-size strategy and convergence analysis that do not assume Lipschitz smoothness. Under weaker assumptions, including a general bounded-variance condition, the resulting method converges while matching current best-known convergence rates. The result broadens the settings covered by theory without claiming that convergence holds without any assumptions.

The analysis includes nonconvex, strongly convex, and convex but not strongly convex objectives. For each category, it covers both random reshuffling and arbitrary shuffling schemes. Numerical experiments also support the method's practical performance. The main contribution is a wider theoretical foundation for shuffling-based optimization, paired with a step-size strategy that preserves strong rates under the stated weaker conditions.
icml-2025-revisiting-convergence-shuffli.tldr: A new step-size strategy gives shuffling-based gradient methods strong convergence rates without assuming Lipschitz smoothness.

paragraphs: Concealed object segmentation seeks objects that visually blend into their surroundings. RUN frames this task as separating foreground from background, with an additional sparsity constraint on the residual to reduce uncertainty. The solution process is unfolded into a network with multiple stages, turning originally fixed optimization parameters into quantities that can be learned.

Each stage has two complementary modules. Segmentation-Oriented Foreground Separation operates on the segmentation mask and uses a Reversible State Space mechanism to capture nonlocal information. Reconstruction-Oriented Background Extraction extends reversible processing into the RGB image domain. Its reconstruction network addresses conflicting foreground and background regions that can arise when independent modules estimate them separately.

Across stages, RUN refines foreground and background modeling in both domains, reducing false-positive and false-negative regions. Experiments report superior performance and support the usefulness of this unfolding-based design for concealed object segmentation. The approach matters because it combines segmentation decisions with image reconstruction, using both to address uncertainty where object appearance is difficult to distinguish from the background.
icml-2025-run-reversible-unfolding-netwo.tldr: RUN unfolds foreground-background separation into a multistage network that refines concealed-object predictions in both mask and RGB domains.

paragraphs: Choosing a step size is an important part of a Frank-Wolfe optimization algorithm: it determines how far to move along an update direction. A full line search can make an effective choice, but the computation spent finding that choice also affects how quickly optimization progresses. This paper focuses on reducing that overhead.

The authors propose a step-size strategy based on the secant method. Under mild assumptions on the objective function, it can be used with any Frank-Wolfe algorithm. The strategy adapts to local smoothness, allowing the step choice to respond to the function's behavior around the current optimization region.

The paper reports effectiveness comparable to full line search with substantially lower computational cost, producing higher effective convergence rates. The authors support the strategy with theoretical guarantees and numerical experiments. Its significance is the connection between useful step choices and the time spent obtaining them: a less expensive search can improve practical progress while retaining the benefits of adapting to the objective's local behavior.
icml-2025-secant-line-search-for-frank-w.tldr: A secant-based step-size strategy offers full-line-search effectiveness at lower computational cost for Frank-Wolfe algorithms under mild assumptions.

paragraphs: Bayesian experimental design concerns choosing experiments as information becomes available. Policy-based approaches can train a design policy before the experiment begins, preparing it to make subsequent choices. This paper asks how that preparation can be combined with further learning during the particular experiment being carried out.

Stepwise Deep Adaptive Design, or Step-DAD, starts with an upfront trained policy, as existing fully amortized approaches do. It then periodically updates that policy using newly gathered data. This is the meaning of its semi-amortized design: the method combines advance training with additional adaptation rather than keeping the learned policy fixed throughout the experiment.

The updates refine the policy to the specific experimental instance, improving the strategy's flexibility and robustness. Empirically, Step-DAD consistently achieves better decision-making and robustness than current state-of-the-art Bayesian experimental design methods in the reported comparisons. The contribution is a way to make experimental design responsive at the policy-learning level, so observations can improve the strategy itself as well as inform the next experimental choice.
icml-2025-step-dad-semi-amortized-policy.tldr: Step-DAD periodically updates a pretrained experimental-design policy as data arrives, improving reported decision-making and robustness.

paragraphs: Activation steering changes a language model's internal computation to influence its behavior. Fixed, manually chosen intervention strengths can make too little correction or push the model too far. Mechanistic Error Reduction with Abstention, or MERA, addresses this by treating the direction, timing, and strength of an intervention as connected decisions.

MERA optimizes the direction of the correction and calibrates whether to apply it and how strongly. When it cannot identify a confident correction, it abstains from intervening. This abstention concerns the steering decision, allowing the framework to avoid forcing a correction simply because an intervention mechanism is available.

The paper provides a principled guarantee of improvement or abstention when confident correction is unavailable. Experiments across several datasets and language-model families demonstrate effective, non-degrading error correction and better results than existing baselines. MERA can also be added to existing steering methods to improve their performance. Its contribution is a selective approach to mechanistic intervention that incorporates the decision to leave the model's computation alone.
icml-2025-to-steer-or-not-to-steer-mecha.tldr: MERA calibrates when and how to steer language-model activations, improving performance or abstaining when no confident correction is available.

paragraphs: Mechanistic interpretability studies computational circuits inside language models to explain their behavior. Task-specific circuit discovery can be difficult to transfer across language tasks, and interpreting individual computational components can require substantial human or advanced-model effort. This paper proposes organizing explanations around reusable functional units that can appear in more than one task.

The proposed modular-circuit vocabulary contains small computational subgraphs paired with interpretations of their functions. Different tasks can share these units, allowing an interpretation established once to be reused. This aims to connect explanations across tasks while reducing the repeated work of interpreting each computational node separately.

The authors introduce five criteria for characterizing such a vocabulary and present ModCirc, a framework for discovering modular circuits in language models. Their evaluations show that the discovered circuits perform well on several metrics. The contribution is a framework for moving toward broader mechanistic explanations through shared components. It provides evidence for reusable modular structure without claiming a complete explanation of every computation in a language model.
icml-2025-towards-global-level-mechanist.tldr: ModCirc discovers reusable, interpreted computational modules to connect language-model explanations across tasks and reduce repeated interpretation work.
